Traffic and parking are major problems in the city's central business district, which has several large office towers. A city plans to cut downtown traffic by raising downtown parking fees by 50 percent. City officials argue that, faced with the higher fees, many drivers who now park downtown will switch to the metro, which stops within a short walk of most downtown offices.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The city last raised its downtown parking fees ten years ago.
Most vehicles entering downtown on weekdays are delivery vans and tradespeople's vehicles carrying equipment, and they cannot do their work by metro.
Downtown parking garages are mostly owned by private operators.
Metro trains on the line serving downtown run every five minutes at peak times.
Some drivers park downtown for less than an hour at a time.
questions.explanation:
A plan relying on drivers' switching. The best weakener shows that many of the drivers can't or won't switch.

**Correct: (B).** These drivers can't use the metro, so the higher fee would not move them to it and traffic wouldn't fall as expected.

(A) The history of fee changes doesn't show whether drivers will switch.

(C) Ownership doesn't change drivers' responses to the fee.

(D) Frequent trains make switching easier, which supports the plan.

(E) Short stays don't show that those drivers would not switch.
questions.tip: Plans that depend on people changing behaviour are weakened by evidence that many can't change.
questions.trap: The "ownership of garages" choice sounds like it matters to fees, but it has no bearing on driver behaviour.

questions.prompt:
The company provides services to businesses and individuals, and it surveys all its customers once a year. A company's annual customer survey shows that the percentage of its customers who are satisfied with its service rose from 60 percent to 75 percent over a three-year period. The company's chief executive concludes that the company now has more satisfied customers than it did three years ago.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Some satisfied customers also use the services of competing companies.
The customer survey is administered by an independent agency.
Most of the company's customers are small businesses.
Customers rate their satisfaction on a five-point scale.
The company's total number of customers shrank by more than one fifth over the three years.
questions.explanation:
The evidence is a percentage; the conclusion is a count. The best weakener shows the base shrank enough to wipe out the gain.

**Correct: (E).** If customers fell by more than a fifth, 75 percent of the smaller base is fewer people than 60 percent of the original.

(A) Using other companies doesn't change how many of this company's customers are satisfied.

(B) Independence supports the survey's reliability.

(C) The type of customer doesn't affect the count of satisfied customers.

(D) The scale doesn't affect the comparison.
questions.tip: Percent up and "more people" are different claims: ask what happened to the total.
questions.trap: The "independent agency" choice seems to challenge the survey, but independence helps it.

questions.prompt:
Both cities are large, with growing populations and significant congestion, and the bike-sharing scheme in Ahmedabad was one of the first of its kind in the country. In Ahmedabad, the introduction of a public bike-sharing scheme was followed by a doubling of daily cycling trips in the city. Planners in Bengaluru argue that introducing a similar scheme in their city will also double the number of daily cycling trips there.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Ahmedabad's scheme took two years to set up.
Bengaluru has more residents than Ahmedabad.
Ahmedabad's scheme was built around a network of protected bike lanes that Bengaluru's roads currently lack.
Bike-sharing schemes operate in many cities around the world.
Several Bengaluru residents already own bicycles.
questions.explanation:
An analogy: what happened in Ahmedabad will happen in Bengaluru. The best weakener points to a relevant difference between the cities.

**Correct: (C).** If the bike lanes were what made cycling attractive, Bengaluru's scheme without them would not produce the same result.

(A) The set-up time doesn't affect the outcome in Bengaluru.

(B) A larger population doesn't show that the scheme would work less well.

(D) Their commonness doesn't show that this one will behave differently.

(E) Ownership could help or make no difference, so it doesn't weaken the claim.
questions.tip: Analogy arguments are weakened by one decisive difference between the cases.
questions.trap: The "more residents" choice sounds like it matters, but size alone doesn't change the mechanism.

questions.prompt:
The company has several offices with outdoor space and has encouraged staff to be active during the working day. A company's health report shows that employees who regularly take walking breaks during the working day are, on average, healthier than those who do not. The company's wellness manager concludes that taking regular walking breaks improves employees' health, and she plans to require every employee to take them.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Employees in poor health often find walking uncomfortable and so take fewer walking breaks.
The average walking break at the company lasts about ten minutes.
Many employees use their walking breaks to make personal phone calls.
Most of the company's employees are covered by health insurance.
The company's walking paths were built only last year.
questions.explanation:
Correlation is read as cause. The weakener flips the arrow: perhaps good health is what lets employees take walks.

**Correct: (A).** Good health may therefore lead to walking breaks rather than the other way round, so forcing breaks on others needn't improve their health.

(B) The length doesn't bear on the direction of cause.

(C) What they do while walking is irrelevant.

(D) Insurance coverage doesn't bear on whether walking improves health.

(E) The age of the paths doesn't show whether walking works.
questions.tip: Whenever a correlation becomes a cause, test the reverse: could the effect be causing the cause?
questions.trap: The phone calls choice sounds like a reason walking might not help, but it doesn't challenge the causal claim.

questions.prompt:
The volunteers were all adults who were overweight and who agreed to keep records of what they ate. A nutrition laboratory recruited 200 volunteers to follow a new "Diet Z" for twelve weeks. The volunteers lost an average of 6 kilograms. The lab concludes that Diet Z is effective for weight loss among adults generally.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The volunteers' average age was 38.
The volunteers were weighed on the same scale each time.
Diet Z includes more vegetables than the typical diet of adults.
Most of the volunteers also began a supervised exercise programme during the twelve weeks.
Diet Z was developed by the same laboratory that ran the study.
questions.explanation:
The weight loss is real; the question is whether Diet Z caused it. The best weakener supplies another reason volunteers would lose weight.

**Correct: (D).** The exercise could explain much of the weight loss, so Diet Z's role is unclear.

(A) Their age doesn't give another cause of weight loss.

(B) This supports the reliability of the measurements.

(C) This could support the diet's effectiveness.

(E) The source of the diet doesn't show that the result is due to something else.
questions.tip: A second change that occurs in the same period is the favourite weakener for treatment studies.
questions.trap: The "developed by the same lab" choice feels like bias, but it doesn't give a specific alternative cause.

questions.prompt:
Rents in the capital have risen quickly in recent years, and many tenants spend a large part of their income on housing. A state government plans to cap rents in its capital city so that more people can afford rented homes. Officials argue that the cap will increase the number of affordable rental homes available in the city.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Rents in the capital have risen faster than wages over the past decade.
Faced with capped rents, many landlords are likely to sell their rental properties or convert them to other uses, reducing the number of homes for rent.
Rent caps have been introduced in several large cities abroad.
Most tenants in the capital say that they support a rent cap.
The cap will be reviewed once a year.
questions.explanation:
The cap lowers the price of rentals, but "the number available" depends on supply. The best weakener points to a side effect on supply.

**Correct: (B).** The plan could shrink supply, defeating its purpose.

(A) This shows the need for action, not that the cap will fail.

(C) The fact of their existence doesn't show how this cap will work.

(D) Tenant support is not evidence of the cap's effect on supply.

(E) An annual review doesn't indicate that supply would fall.
questions.tip: For price controls, test the effect on supply.
questions.trap: The "rents rose faster than wages" choice sounds like it weakens, but it supports the need for the plan.

questions.prompt:
The retailer has about a hundred stores and has encouraged customers to use the app to see offers and track their purchases. A retailer's study found that customers who use its mobile app spend, on average, 20 percent more per month in its stores than customers who do not. The retailer concludes that using the app leads customers to spend more in its stores, and it plans a large campaign to get more customers to download the app.

Each of the following, if true, weakens the retailer's argument EXCEPT:
choices: Before the app was launched, the customers who later downloaded it were already the retailer's highest spenders.
The 20 percent difference is largely the result of a few very large purchases made by a small number of app users.
Many customers download the app only when they are about to make a large purchase, to claim a discount offered through it.
App users earn loyalty points only on in-store purchases, so they buy staples in the stores that other customers buy online.
Customers who started using the app spent noticeably more in the stores than they had spent in the months before they started using it.
questions.explanation:
This is an EXCEPT question: four choices weaken the claim that the app causes more spending, and one does not. The correct choice strengthens the claim or is neutral.

**Correct: (E).** This is a before-and-after comparison within the same customers, which supports the retailer's causal claim, so it does not weaken.

(A) Weakens: the high spenders may simply have been the ones to download it.

(B) Weakens: the average is not typical of app users in general.

(C) Weakens: the app is a result of planned spending, not a cause.

(D) Weakens: the difference could reflect where the spending takes place rather than a rise in spending.
questions.tip: For EXCEPT questions, label each choice W or N; the odd one is the answer.
questions.trap: Choosing a weakener because it sounds negative; the answer is the one that helps the author.

questions.prompt:
Colon cancer is a common disease, and the screening programme is available free of charge to eligible people across the country. A health ministry reports that the five-year survival rate for people diagnosed with colon cancer rose from 55 percent to 65 percent in the years after a national screening programme was introduced. The ministry concludes that the screening programme has improved patients' chances of surviving the disease.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The programme invites everyone aged fifty and over to be screened.
The screening test is painless and takes only a few minutes.
Colon cancer is the third most common cancer in the country.
Screening detects cancers earlier in their development, so patients are diagnosed sooner and counted as five-year survivors, even if they die at the same age as before.
Screening programmes for other cancers are being expanded.
questions.explanation:
Survival rates are measured from the date of diagnosis. If screening finds cancers earlier, patients get a longer "survival clock" even if they die at the same age. The weakener should exploit that.

**Correct: (D).** Earlier diagnosis can raise the five-year figure without anyone living longer, so the conclusion isn't supported.

(A) Who is invited doesn't challenge the claim about survival.

(B) Comfort of the test is irrelevant.

(C) Prevalence doesn't bear on whether screening improved survival.

(E) Other programmes are out of scope.
questions.tip: Survival measured from diagnosis can be inflated by earlier diagnosis alone ("lead-time" effect).
questions.trap: The "invites everyone over fifty" choice describes the programme, not why the survival numbers might be misleading.

questions.prompt:
The children came from a range of schools in one region, and the researchers also collected information on the children's family backgrounds. In a study of 1,000 children, those who began learning a musical instrument before the age of eight scored higher on language tests at age twelve than those who did not. The researchers conclude that early instrument training boosts children's language abilities.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The language tests measured vocabulary and grammar.
Parents who enrol their children in early music lessons are, on average, more highly educated and more likely to read to their children daily, and daily reading strongly predicts language scores.
Some children in the study stopped taking music lessons before the age of twelve.
Children who began lessons before eight practised for an average of thirty minutes a day.
The piano was the most common instrument among the children in the study.
questions.explanation:
A correlation, causal reading. The best weakener offers a factor that would plausibly lead both to early music lessons and to language skill.

**Correct: (B).** Home reading offers a competing cause for the language scores, and it is linked to the choice of early music lessons.

(A) What the tests measured doesn't challenge the causal link.

(C) Dropping out later doesn't give an alternative cause.

(D) Practice time, if anything, supports the training claim.

(E) The type of instrument is irrelevant.
questions.tip: The best weakener for a correlation is a third factor that plausibly drives both variables.
questions.trap: The "stopped lessons" choice seems to threaten the training effect, but doesn't suggest a rival cause.

questions.prompt:
The company sells software to businesses across the country, and its sales staff have traditionally visited clients in person. A company plans to replace most client visits by its sales staff with video calls, to cut travel costs. Management argues that sales will not suffer, because in a six-month pilot in one region, where salespeople used video calls for most client contact, sales were unchanged.

Each of the following, if true, weakens the management's argument EXCEPT:
choices: The pilot region consists mainly of the company's oldest clients, with whom it has long-standing relationships.
Most of the company's new-client wins in other regions come from in-person visits.
Competitors in the other regions have increased their in-person visits to clients.
Clients in the other regions are, on average, less comfortable with video calls than clients in the pilot region.
The video-calling software the sales staff would use costs less than a tenth of the travel savings.
questions.explanation:
An EXCEPT question: four choices weaken the claim that video calls will not hurt sales; the odd one supports it or is irrelevant.

**Correct: (E).** This is about the cost of the plan and says nothing about whether sales will suffer, so it doesn't weaken the argument.

(A) Weakens: relationships that already exist survive without visits; new or different clients may not.

(B) Weakens: the plan would remove the very activity that wins new business.

(C) Weakens: the company could lose ground to rivals who visit.

(D) Weakens: the pilot result may not carry over to clients who respond differently.
questions.tip: In EXCEPT questions, don't look for the best answer; look for the one that does no damage.
questions.trap: Picking one of the four weakeners because it's the "worst" statement for the company.

questions.prompt:
Advanced driver-assistance features include lane-keeping aids and automatic emergency braking, and insurers have been collecting data on accident claims. In a survey of 10,000 drivers, owners of cars fitted with advanced driver-assistance features had 25 percent fewer accidents per 100,000 kilometres driven than owners of cars without such features. An insurance executive concludes that the driver-assistance features reduce the number of accidents.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The features cost an extra one and a half lakh rupees on most models.
Some owners of equipped cars switch the features off.
Drivers who buy cars with these features tend to drive mostly on motorways, where accident rates per kilometre are much lower than on city roads.
The accident data come from police reports and insurance claims.
The surveyed drivers were chosen from several states.
questions.explanation:
The measure is accidents per kilometre, which depends heavily on where and how people drive. The best weakener gives owners of equipped cars a safer driving profile that has nothing to do with the features.

**Correct: (C).** Their lower accident rate could be due to where they drive, not to the features.

(A) Price doesn't affect how many accidents occur.

(B) Owners who switch them off would, if anything, dilute the apparent effect, so the true effect of the features might be even larger.

(D) The data sources are a normal basis, and the choice doesn't challenge the conclusion.

(E) Geographical spread doesn't weaken the claim.
questions.tip: When rates are compared, look for differences in exposure (distance, road type) between the groups.
questions.trap: The "owners switch them off" choice looks like an attack on the features but works in the opposite direction.

questions.prompt:
The country's economy relies on manufacturing, and its officials are looking for ways to increase foreign earnings. The government of a country plans to devalue its currency in order to increase export earnings. Officials argue that the devaluation will make the country's goods cheaper for foreign buyers, so that export volumes will rise enough to raise total export earnings.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Most of the country's export industries depend heavily on components imported and paid for in foreign currency, so devaluation raises their costs by nearly as much as it lowers the foreign price of their goods.
The country's currency has been devalued twice in the past thirty years.
Exports account for a small share of the country's total economic output.
Several of the country's trading partners have strong currencies.
Foreign buyers generally prefer lower prices to higher prices.
questions.explanation:
Devaluation lowers the foreign price of exports. But the plan's effect on earnings depends on what happens to the exporters' costs and to volume. The best weakener breaks the link between a cheaper currency and cheaper goods.

**Correct: (A).** Higher costs would offset the price advantage, so export volumes and earnings may not rise.

(B) The history of devaluations doesn't show that this one will fail.

(C) The plan is about export earnings, and the size of exports in the economy doesn't change the effect.

(D) Strong partner currencies would, if anything, help the plan.

(E) This supports the plan.
questions.tip: If a plan relies on a price falling, ask whether the seller's costs would rise to match.
questions.trap: The "small share of output" choice sounds like an economic limit, but the argument is about export earnings, not total output.

questions.prompt:
The town has about eighty thousand residents, and the mayor reviewed the year's figures at a public meeting. After a town installed brighter street lights along its main roads, crime in the town fell by 15 percent over the following year. The mayor concludes that the brighter lights reduced crime.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The new lights cost the town two crore rupees to install.
Residents say they like the brighter lights.
The new lights use less electricity than the old ones.
In the same year, the town doubled the number of police officers patrolling its main roads.
The town is smaller than most neighbouring towns.
questions.explanation:
A before-and-after causal claim. A second change at the same time provides an alternative cause.

**Correct: (D).** More patrols could explain the fall in crime, so the lights may have played no part.

(A) Cost doesn't affect the cause of the fall.

(B) Liking isn't evidence about crime.

(C) Energy use is irrelevant to crime.

(E) Size doesn't give another cause. In weaken questions the best answer usually names a concrete second change that happened at the same time as the supposed cause, so you can ask whether the effect would have happened even without the lights. Choices about cost, popularity or the size of the town never give such a rival cause.
questions.tip: Look for a concurrent change that could also explain the effect.
questions.trap: The electricity choice sounds like a fact about the lights, but doesn't touch the crime claim.

questions.prompt:
The chain, which sells coffee and snacks, is considering whether to switch to ethically sourced beans in all its stores. A coffee chain surveyed 500 customers at its flagship Mumbai store and found that 70 percent would pay a little extra for coffee made from ethically sourced beans. The chain's marketing manager concludes that most of its customers across India would pay extra for such coffee.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The chain operates more than a hundred stores across India.
Customers at the Mumbai flagship store are, on average, considerably wealthier than customers at the chain's other stores.
Ethically sourced beans cost the chain about fifteen percent more than other beans.
The survey was carried out on a weekday morning.
Many customers at the flagship store visit the store daily.
questions.explanation:
The sample is one store's customers, the conclusion covers every store. A weakener shows that this store's customers are unusual.

**Correct: (B).** Wealthier customers are likelier to accept a higher price, so the result may not carry over.

(A) The number of stores doesn't show that the flagship's customers differ.

(C) The chain's cost doesn't affect customer willingness.

(D) Timing is not obviously relevant to opinions on ethically sourced beans.

(E) Frequent visits don't show that those customers differ from others in willingness to pay.
questions.tip: One-site sample, nationwide claim: look for a difference between the site and the rest.
questions.trap: The "more than a hundred stores" choice sounds like a scale problem, but only a difference in customers would weaken.

questions.prompt:
The centre employs about eight hundred people who handle calls and emails from customers, and the company is reviewing its costs. A company plans to move its customer-support centre from Gurugram to a smaller city where salaries are about 30 percent lower. The company's finance head argues that the move will reduce the centre's overall operating costs.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Salaries in Gurugram have risen about eight percent a year recently.
The smaller city has fewer restaurants than Gurugram.
The smaller city's airport has few direct flights.
Several of the company's competitors have support centres in Gurugram.
Staff turnover in the smaller city is much higher, and the cost of recruiting and training replacements would exceed the salary savings.
questions.explanation:
Salary is one cost among several. The weakener should show that the move triggers other costs that outweigh the saving.

**Correct: (E).** Extra hiring and training costs could cancel the saving and even raise total costs.

(A) This supports the plan by increasing the saving.

(B) Restaurants have no bearing on the centre's operating costs.

(C) The centre isn't described as depending on flights.

(D) Competitors' locations don't change the company's costs. The general lesson is that a measurement taken at two different times is only a fair comparison if conditions were the same, so a difference in conditions between the two surveys is a strong attack on the conclusion.
questions.tip: When a plan cuts one cost, look for a cost it adds.
questions.trap: The "salaries rising" choice relates to salaries, but it strengthens the plan.

questions.prompt:
The company has about two thousand employees and carries out the satisfaction survey twice a year with every employee. A company introduced a "no-meeting Wednesday" policy. In the employee survey that followed, the average satisfaction score rose from 62 to 71. The human-resources head concludes that the policy raised employee satisfaction.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The policy was introduced in response to requests from employees.
Some employees still attend meetings on Wednesdays.
The first survey was taken during the busy quarter-end, and the second during a quiet holiday period.
The satisfaction survey contains twenty questions.
The company has about three thousand employees.
questions.explanation:
Two survey scores are compared. The weakener should show that something other than the policy could have moved the scores, such as when the surveys were taken.

**Correct: (C).** Workload and mood differ at the two times, so the rise could reflect the timing rather than the policy.

(A) This suggests the policy fits employees' wishes, which might support the claim.

(B) A few exceptions don't undermine the overall effect.

(D) The length of the survey doesn't explain the change.

(E) Company size is irrelevant.
questions.tip: Compare-measurement arguments are weakened when the two measurements were taken under different conditions.
questions.trap: The "policy introduced at employees' request" choice sounds relevant but supports rather than weakens.

questions.prompt:
The chain operates about two hundred stores around the country, and the programme was introduced to improve customer service. A retail chain gave its ten worst-performing stores a new staff-training programme. Sales at those stores rose by an average of 12 percent in the following year. The chain's operations director concludes that the training programme works and recommends rolling it out to all stores.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The ten stores had been selected because their sales were unusually low the year before, a year in which several of them suffered temporary disruptions such as flooding and road works.
The programme cost about two lakh rupees per store.
Managers at all ten stores attended the training in person.
The ten stores were located in different regions of the country.
Sales at the ten stores had been below the chain's average for the previous year.
questions.explanation:
The stores were picked because they did badly. Extreme results often drift back toward normal without any intervention, and a one-off bad year can be a fluke.

**Correct: (A).** Their sales may simply have recovered once the disruptions ended, so the training need not have caused the rise.

(B) Cost is irrelevant to whether sales rose because of the training.

(C) This supports the programme, if anything.

(D) Spread across regions doesn't give a rival explanation.

(E) This is already implied by their selection, and it doesn't offer a specific reason for recovery.
questions.tip: If a group was selected for being at an extreme, expect "regression to the mean" as a weakener.
questions.trap: The "below the chain's average" choice is merely a restatement of how the stores were chosen.

questions.prompt:
The city is one of the country's largest, and its restaurant sector is an important source of employment. An economist argues that the 15 percent fall in the number of new restaurants opened in a large city last year shows that the city's economy is weakening. She notes that restaurant openings have generally been a good indicator of business confidence.

Each of the following, if true, weakens the economist's argument EXCEPT:
choices: A new licensing procedure introduced last year caused long delays in approving restaurant openings.
Many restaurant owners expanded existing restaurants instead of opening new ones.
A zoning change sharply reduced the number of commercial properties available for restaurants.
Over the same period, the number of existing restaurants that closed rose sharply.
In this city, restaurant openings have historically shown little relationship to the growth of the wider economy.
questions.explanation:
An EXCEPT question: four choices give another reason for fewer openings or undermine the indicator; the odd one backs the economist or is neutral.

**Correct: (D).** Rising closures suggest that business conditions in the sector are worsening, which supports her view.

(A) Weakens: the fall may reflect red tape, not weak confidence.

(B) Weakens: investment may have gone into expansion, not shrunk.

(C) Weakens: a shortage of premises explains fewer openings.

(E) Weakens: the indicator she relies on isn't reliable here.
questions.tip: Use W and N tags for each choice; the exception is the one tagged N (or S).
questions.trap: Treating "closures rose" as a weakener because it sounds like a different fact about restaurants.

questions.prompt:
The study covered several hundred firms across a number of countries, using data on employees who left voluntarily. Researchers found that the rate of employee turnover is lower at firms that offer flexible working hours. After controlling for firm size, industry and average pay, they still found the difference. They conclude that offering flexible hours reduces employee turnover.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Larger firms are more likely than smaller firms to offer flexible hours.
Well-managed firms are more likely to offer flexible hours and also tend to have lower turnover, for reasons that have nothing to do with the hours.
Firms in the technology industry are more likely than others to offer flexible hours.
Firms that pay above-average salaries tend to have lower turnover.
Some employees at firms that offer flexible hours never use them.
questions.explanation:
The researchers have already removed three obvious alternative explanations. A good weakener must be a new one that none of those controls cover.

**Correct: (B).** Management quality could drive both, and it wasn't controlled for.

(A) Firm size was already controlled for.

(C) Industry was already controlled for.

(D) Pay was already controlled for.

(E) This might dilute the effect but doesn't give a rival explanation for the lower turnover. The general lesson is that when researchers say what they have controlled for, the correct weakener must be a factor outside that list, and one that could plausibly influence both flexible hours and turnover.
questions.tip: If a stimulus says what's been controlled for, the weakener will be something else.
questions.trap: Picking an alternative cause that the researchers have already controlled for.

questions.prompt:
A city water utility plans to introduce tiered pricing: the first 10,000 litres a household uses each month will be cheap, and each litre beyond that will cost much more. The utility argues that the city's total household water consumption will fall, because households that now use more than 10,000 litres a month will cut back to avoid the higher rate.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Households that use more than 10,000 litres a month account for most of the water the utility sells.
Tiered pricing systems are used by water utilities in several other cities.
Some households that use less than 10,000 litres a month will use slightly more because the first tier is cheap.
The utility's revenue will increase after the new prices take effect.
Most households now using more than 10,000 litres a month are large joint families whose use is already close to the minimum needed for drinking, cooking and sanitation.
questions.explanation:
The plan counts on heavy users cutting back. The best weakener shows that heavy users can't really cut back, so the mechanism fails.

**Correct: (E).** Households that are already near the minimum can't cut back much, so the expected fall in consumption won't occur.

(A) This shows that their behaviour matters, which supports the plan.

(B) Common use doesn't show that it fails here.

(C) A small rise at the low end offsets only part of the expected fall and doesn't remove the mechanism for heavy users.

(D) Revenue is a different matter from total consumption.
questions.tip: If a plan expects a group to change behaviour, a weakener shows that they cannot.
questions.trap: The "low-use households use slightly more" choice is half-right, but it only partly offsets the effect.
